newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Hold-up of Albania premier underscores chaos.
newsitem.headline: Hold-up of Albania premier underscores chaos.

text.p: An armed hold-up of Albania's prime minister underscored the chaos in the Balkan state as it awaited the arrival of an Italian-led multinational security force to secure aid supplies.
Prime Minister Bashkim Fino was forced to abandon plans to visit a northern city after about 15 armed men stopped a convoy of cars in which he was travelling with three other government ministers.
Fino, 34, vowed nevertheless that his all-party crisis government would press ahead undaunted with a programme including June elections under a deal last month aimed at ending an armed uprising.
"This does not frighten us at all," he said. "The government of national reconciliation will work day and night to restore order."
But the evidence of no-go areas for the prime minister indicated that lawlessness and banditry might easily intimidate politicians and voters in the run-up to the planned poll in June.

It showed the power of gunmen in a country where all political parties favour quick deployment of the Italian-led security force of up to 6,000 troops to safeguard shipments of food and medical supplies.
U.N. relief agencies estimate that 400,000 of Albania's 3.4 million people will run out of food soon if nothing is done.

Italy, which says the force will start to arrive in the week of April 14, is expected to provide 2,000 to 2,500 troops, France 1,000, Greece 700, Turkey 500, Romania 400 and Spain 300. Austria and Denmark may also take part.

Fino, a former socialist mayor of a southern Albanian town, ordered an investigation into the ambush in which the gunmen detonated two roadside grenades and fired into the air near Bushat, 100 km (60 miles) north of Tirana. No one was hurt.
Right-wing President Sali Berisha, who agreed under pressure to Fino's appointment at the head of a unity government on March 11, has his strongest support in northern Albania.

Finance Minister Arben Malaj, who was with Fino, said the gunmen claimed 120 people from the northern town of Shkoder were being held in the southern port of Sarande and demanded their release. He said the government would check whether the claim was true.

Most of southern Albania, including Sarande, is run by rebel councils demanding Berisha's resignation after protests over the collapse of popular savings schemes erupted into an armed uprising last month. Arms depots were looted and banditry is now rife.
Berisha, reiterating the government's backing for the security force, took a swipe at the southern rebels.

"The international forces, including the Italian troops, will have the support of Albanian official, central and local authorities," the state news agency said he told a visiting Italian parliamentarian.
"But this does not rule out any eventual danger as long as in several zones of southern Albania there are still some irresponsible armed gangs."
